(Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- docs-consistency-guard: Documentation agent that audits docs for staleness and inconsistency AND generates/updates documentation on request. Use proactively when reviewing any PR that touches CLAUDE.md, docs/adr/, CONTRIBUTING.md, or docs/architecture.md. Also invoke when the user asks "is the documentation up to date?", "update the milestone", "scaffold the ADR for X", "add this to the ADR index", "add a TODO item", "scaffold a README for X", or "create a doc stub for Y." (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Write, Edit)

- driver-boundary-guard: Specialized reviewer for values that cross a DRIVER boundary — anything DataQ receives from a database connector, pyiceberg, pandas/pyarrow, or a cloud SDK and then type-narrows (isinstance / dtype checks / hasattr). Audits whether the covering tests hand-build the value in the shape our model expects (the "fixture encodes our model" defect that hid (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository. (Tools: Bash)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- migration-safety: Specialized reviewer for Alembic migrations under backend/alembic/versions/. Audits for backward-incompatible operations that would break running code during a deploy, per working-agreement (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- orchestration-abstraction-guard: Specialized reviewer that audits backend code for provider-specific branching that bypasses the OrchestrationProvider abstraction. Use this proactively when reviewing any PR that touches backend/app/orchestration/, backend/app/services/, or backend/app/api/ — especially any code path handling ADF or Airflow events, trigger bindings, or pipeline_runs. Also invoke when the user asks "does this go through the abstraction?" or similar. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>

<example>

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- qa-verifier: QA/QE agent that (1) runs the full local verification battery mirroring CI's required checks before any commit/push/PR, (2) audits test quality on changed code — failure-mode coverage, mocked-seam smells, coverage on changed files (Week-8 ≥80% gate), and (3) exercises the running application with data-level scenarios — authoring suites/checks through the real API, negative and edge-case inputs, authz probes — against the local stack's seeded demo data. Use proactively before pushing a branch or opening a PR, after writing or modifying tests, or when the user asks "run the gate", "is this ready to push?", "is this tested enough?", or "smoke the app with bad data". (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- regression-mutation-verifier: Proves that a new regression test actually fails against the unfixed code. Reverts the fix inside a throwaway git worktree, runs only the new test, and reports whether it fails for the RIGHT reason — catching tests that pass no matter what (the (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Edit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- ui-tester: End-to-end UI QA agent that exercises DataQ's frontend on BOTH desktop and mobile viewports (functionality + rendering) against the running app, AND audits backend↔frontend feature parity — flagging backend capabilities with no frontend surface (and frontend calls with no backend). Use when the user asks to "test the UI", "check mobile rendering", "find backend/frontend gaps", "is this feature wired end-to-end", or before a release. # Microsoft Learn MCP Server

This server gives structured access to official Microsoft and Azure documentation via three tools:

## Tools

### microsoft_docs_search
Search official documentation and return up to 10 concise, high-quality content chunks (max 500 tokens each), including title, URL, and excerpt.

- Use first to get a quick, reliable overview
- Ideal for grounding answers in Microsoft knowledge

### microsoft_code_sample_search
Search for code snippets and examples in official Microsoft Learn documentation and return up to 20 relevant, high-quality code samples.

- Use when you need to provide sample Microsoft/Azure related code in your answers.  
- Ideal for generating code snippets or practical implementation examples.  
- Optional parameter `language` can filter results. 

### microsoft_docs_fetch
Fetch and convert full Microsoft documentation pages to markdown.

- Use after search when you need full content from a specific URL
- Required for detailed tutorials, troubleshooting, prerequisites, code samples, or when search results are incomplete or outdated

## Workflow

1. Use `microsoft_docs_search` to find relevant documents.
2. If you need code examples or practical snippets, use `microsoft_code_sample_search`.
3. If deeper or complete information is needed, use `microsoft_docs_fetch`.

**Search gives breadth. Code Sample Search gives practical examples. Fetch gives depth.**

All content comes from Microsoft Learn or official sources, returned in clean markdown format.

The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

lock mechanism moved into a shared `services/connection_lock.py` rather than being written twice,

PERMISSION classification was a broad substring match applied regardless of *when* the failure

that was never the problem while the real fault stayed undiagnosed (a confident wrong answer, the

OUT of `inventory_sync` — at UPDATE time, not only in the daily sweep, since the sweep can't see
the toggled-off-and-back-on-between-ticks window and every reader would meanwhile be told "failing
since <old date>" for a sync nobody has attempted since.

**#1179/#1201 is the #953 shape again** — `docs/feature-matrix.md`'s custom-SQL-on-UC tick had

column/table expectations, which work fine on a DataFrame batch. Feature-matrix entry corrected
to say so rather than quietly re-ticked.

PRs (CLAUDE.md §11 — don't batch unrelated changes into one commit): five into `v1.1 Backlog` —

(`unexpected_index_list` uncapped at capture time on pandas-backed datasources),
[#1197](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1197) (redaction label can undercount
vs. what's actually rendered), [#1199](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1199)
(surface the env near-miss signal in-product, not just the DB) — and three into the open
`v1.1 Week 6` milestone since they surfaced live, W6-adjacent work:
[#1200](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1200) (non-hermetic
`test_seed_otp_operator_share` reads the ambient `DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL`),
[#1202](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1202) (custom-SQL checks have no
`metric_value`, only JSONB `observed_value` — no trend/anomaly baseline),
[#1203](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1203) (a GX SQL-batch exception message
can carry target cell data into `results.observed_value`, outside the column policy).

**Late seventh fix, same day:** the user reported the run-detail **Observed** column still
unbounded — the one column PR #1185's review had scoped out as "verified-benign" on the
assumption `observed_value` is always a compact scalar, which is false for the monitor
kinds (`schema_drift` added/removed/type_changed lists and `comparison` per-column buckets
scale with column count). Filed as
[#1207](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1207) (with the correction posted
on #1184's record), fixed by PR
[#1208](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1208) (same width + ellipsis +
tooltip pattern, keeping `ScalarValue`'s rendering in cell and tooltip; the `Check`/
`Expectation` siblings were verified-benign on the record — DB-capped `String(256)`/
`String(128)` scalars). Five-dimension review: one process finding (the sibling-audit
record, dispositioned in the review comment), zero code defects. **Not yet deployed** —
prod's cut is `7018d772`; #1208 rides the next Deploy run.

### Inventory-sync failure visibility (2026-08-08)

[#1104](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1104) (filed by the #1103 code review,
`v1.1 Backlog`) — an opted-in inventory sync (`config.inventory_sync`, ADR 0040) whose principal
can't read the enumeration query (UC: no `SELECT` on `system.information_schema`; Snowflake:
revoked INFORMATION_SCHEMA access) failed every daily tick invisibly: toggle on, connection test
green (the `SELECT 1` probe never exercises this query), zero assets ever appear, no surface says
why — the #828 shape again. Fixed by PR
[#1227](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1227): three nullable `connections` columns
(`inventory_sync_last_attempted_at`/`inventory_sync_last_error`/`inventory_sync_failing_since`,
migration `c22fa93eb834`, mirroring the `lineage_last_*` pattern from #858) + a
`classify_inventory_sync_error` classifier that names the known system schema for a permission
failure + a connections-list "inventory sync failing" badge for opted-in, currently-failing
connections. Migration tested up/down/up locally against a real Postgres.

The `/code-review` pass on the PR found four real robustness defects in the bookkeeping — all
fixed in-PR, all mutation-checked (each new regression test was re-run against the un-fixed code
to prove it fails for the right reason). Every one turned a **per-connection** failure into a
**per-sweep** one, i.e. the fix for an invisible failure had itself acquired an invisible failure:
(1) the outcome `session.commit()` sat unguarded inside the per-connection `except`, so a
transient Postgres error on the bookkeeping write propagated out of the loop and skipped every
remaining connection; (2) `inventory_sync_failing_since` was a read-modify-write with no row lock,
so two overlapping sweeps both read NULL and both wrote their own "now", walking the START of a
failure streak forward and under-reporting how long a connection had been broken; (3) the except
block read `connection.type` and wrote back to the ORM instance immediately after
`session.rollback()` had expired it — a connection deleted mid-sweep (reachable: an admin deleting
it through the API) raised `ObjectDeletedError` and killed the task. (1)–(3) are the same shape
`orchestration_service.record_poll_failure` already solved for `consecutive_poll_failures`, so the
lock mechanism moved into a shared `services/connection_lock.py` rather than being written twice,
and the outcome write now re-fetches by id under `FOR UPDATE` and never raises. (4) the
PERMISSION classification was a broad substring match applied regardless of *when* the failure
happened, so a secret-store 403 or an expired token — failures that never reached the warehouse —
were reported as "missing SELECT grant on the system schema", sending an admin to fix a privilege
that was never the problem while the real fault stayed undiagnosed (a confident wrong answer, the
exact #828 shape this feature exists to end). The specific message is now gated on PHASE: only a
failure raised by the enumeration query itself (`InventorySyncEnumerationError`, wrapping nothing
but the phase) can claim a grant, and it hedges ("most likely … if the grant is already in place,
re-check the credentials"). Plus a minor: the three columns are now cleared when a connection opts
OUT of `inventory_sync` — at UPDATE time, not only in the daily sweep, since the sweep can't see
the toggled-off-and-back-on-between-ticks window and every reader would meanwhile be told "failing
since <old date>" for a sync nobody has attempted since.

A second review pass on the fixes found four more, all fixed in the same PR: the classifier's
generic fallbacks are written for a RUN, so an inventory failure rendered as "the run failed to
execute. See the server logs" (the answer #1104 exists to replace) and pointed at "the suite's run
target", which a sync does not have — `CONFIG`/`UNKNOWN` now have sync-specific wording while
`CONNECTIVITY`, already datasource-centric, stays shared; the grant message asserted more than the
phase gate can know (a Snowflake role that lost USAGE on its warehouse is rejected at the same
point and reads identically), so it now names the role/warehouse privileges alongside the SELECT
grant; and `deploy/README.md`'s operator row still documented the log-only behaviour. The one
finding deferred is [#1242](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1242): Snowflake's
`INFORMATION_SCHEMA` is **privilege-filtered rather than access-denied**, so a role with no grants
enumerates ZERO ROWS instead of raising — which this PR records as a healthy sync, leaving the
Snowflake half of #1104 exactly where it started. Deferred rather than fixed because an

content.content:
=== #595 ===
[OPEN] Scale-aware execution: sampling / partition-aware checks for the flat-file + UC runners (G-b)
Gap G-b (post-v1-roadmap maturity assessment) — the flat-file + UC runners load the whole file/table into worker pandas; a 100M-row table = worker OOM. The Snowflake path pushes down via SQL and is fine (reference baseline captured in #587 before the subscription lapsed).

**Scope (named workstream under Theme 7):**
- **Row-cap / sampling strategy** per suite or per run-target: head-N, random-sample, and (flat-file) per-file/partition batching via the existing batch-resolution machinery — with the sampled-ness recorded on the result (a check that passed on a sample must say so).
- **UC:** push what's pushable down to Spark/SQL before collecting (freshness/volume/schema_drift monitors never need the full table; expectation subsets that can run as SQL should).
- **Guardrail:** a size probe + configurable hard cap so the worker refuses-with-`error` instead of OOMing.
- **Perf batch same week:** #327 (profiler N+1) + #323 (retention-sweep index/batch) — same theme, same harness.
- Testable cloud-independently: local files at parameterized volume (HARNESS_TODO §6 generator) + Databricks Free for UC.

Incremental (delta-only) validation stays a follow-up — design it, don't build it here.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Sampling strategies (head-N / random) + per-partition/file batching for the flat-file runner; UC pushes monitors + SQL-able subsets down before any collect
- [ ] Size probe + configurable hard cap → run ends `error` with a clear message instead of worker OOM
- [ ] Sampled-ness recorded on the result and visible in the UI (a pass on a sample says so)
- [ ] Volume test vs the #587 Snowflake baseline documented

_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

=== #327 ===
[OPEN] perf(profiler): batch the N+1 per-column top-values warehouse queries
Split out of #147 (item 4) so that issue can close — the other four cleanup items are resolved/confirmed there.

`profile_table` ([profile_service.py](backend/app/services/profile_service.py)) issues 1 aggregate query + **one top-values query per column** in a Python loop. For a 50-column profile that's 51 sequential warehouse round-trips; against a cold SQL warehouse (~1s/query) that's ~50s of wall time for an interactive authoring aid.

Acceptable for v1 (≤50-col cap, and the aggregate query is a single round-trip), so this is **post-v1 perf**, not a correctness bug.

### Why not done now
- Explicitly conditional in #147: "consider batching … **if profiler latency becomes a problem**."
- A safe rewrite (e.g. `UNION ALL` of per-column grouped+limited subqueries, one round-trip) mixes differently-typed `value` columns into one projection, which coerces per-dialect — genuinely risky across both Snowflake and Databricks, and **live warehouse runs are still the deferred Week-1 smoke**, so there's no integration test to catch a regression.

### When to pick up
Once a live warehouse smoke exists (so the batched SQL can be validated end-to-end), or if profiler latency is reported in practice. Keep the per-column builder as the fallback for dialects where the batched form misbehaves.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Profiler top-values collected in batched queries (O(1)–O(2) per table, not per column)
- [ ] Before/after timing recorded; behavior unchanged (tests)

_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

=== #323 ===
[OPEN] Index + batch the result-retention sweep for large results tables
Follow-up from the A8 result-retention sweep (`run_service.purge_expired_sample_failures`, daily `purge_sample_failures` beat task). Surfaced by `/code-review` on the retention PR. Functionality is correct and tested; these are scale optimizations deferred to keep the PR to one functionality.

### 1. No index supports the sweep predicate
The daily `UPDATE results SET sample_failures=NULL, sample_failures_purged_at=now WHERE created_at < cutoff AND sample_failures_purged_at IS NULL AND jsonb_typeof(sample_failures) NOT IN (NULL,'null')` filters on `created_at` + `sample_failures_purged_at`, but `results.__table_args__` indexes only `run_id` and `check_id`. `results` grows by one row per check per run with no row-delete (ADR 0012 keeps `metric_value`), so the sweep does a full sequential scan of an unbounded table every day to scrub a small set.

**Fix:** a backward-compatible Alembic migration adding a partial index, e.g.
`CREATE INDEX ix_results_unpurged_created ON results (created_at) WHERE sample_failures_purged_at IS NULL;`
(tested up/down locally per the migration checklist). The partial predicate keeps the index tiny — it only covers not-yet-purged rows.

### 2. First run on an aged DB does one large unbounded UPDATE
The sweep is a single `UPDATE ... WHERE` with no `LIMIT`/batching. On first run after enabling retention (or after a long outage), it can rewrite a large backlog in one transaction — long row locks + WAL/dead-tuple pressure, briefly contending with concurrent result inserts. The schedule dispatcher deliberately processes one row at a time with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` to avoid exactly this.

**Fix:** batch the purge (e.g. loop `UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id ... LIMIT N)` until 0 rows) so each transaction is bounded. Steady-state matches are small, so this only matters for the catch-up run.

### Not changed (intentional)
- `synchronize_session=False` was already applied on the PR (the `auto`→`fetch` fallback was emitting an extra SELECT-of-PKs).

_Filed per the working agreement: review findings deferred from a PR are tracked, never silently dropped._

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Retention sweep uses an index + batched deletes/updates; runtime on a large seeded `results` table measured
- [ ] No lock-contention regression (documented check)

_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

=== #318 ===
[OPEN] Run progress is binary 0%→100% (GX atomic batch) — no true per-check incremental progress
Surfaced during the /code-review of PR #315 (live run-progress drawer, A3). Pre-existing limitation, not introduced by that PR — filing so it isn't lost.

`run_service.get_run_progress` derives `completed_checks`/`counts` from the presence of `Result` rows. Because GX validates a suite in **one atomic batch**, all result rows land together at completion — so for any non-trivial suite the live-progress bar reads `0 / N` (0%) for the entire run, then jumps to `N / N` (100%) at the terminal transition. The endpoint reports **lifecycle + final per-check resolution**, not sub-GX incremental progress (documented in the `get_run_progress` docstring).

This contradicts the UX intent the consuming code advertises ("watches it execute check-by-check" — [Suites.tsx](frontend/src/pages/Suites.tsx) onRun comment): a long run will read as hung at 0% until it finishes.

**Options (all post-v1, non-trivial):**
- Per-check execution (split the GX batch / run validations incrementally) so rows land as checks complete — biggest change, touches the runner.
- A spinner-only "running" affordance for multi-check suites instead of a 0% bar, to avoid the "hung" read.
- Surface an elapsed-time / heartbeat instead of a misleading percentage while `completed_checks == 0`.

Tie-in: the `freshness`/`volume` monitor-kinds (ADR 0012) and any non-GX runner may not be atomic-batch, so a per-runner progress contract is the deeper fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Run progress reports per-check/per-partition increments instead of binary 0%→100% (natural once #595's partitioned execution lands — ride that work)
- [ ] Live-progress drawer reflects the increments; progress endpoint contract unchanged or versioned
- [ ] Tests cover multi-partition progress sequencing

_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

=== #310 ===
[OPEN] decision (ADR): history/audit strategy — check-version history lost on delete, no audit log, no soft-delete
## Context

The internal Postgres data has **no general SCD/history framework** — it's Alembic for schema + targeted mechanisms. The history/audit review found:

1. **Check version history is lost on delete.** `check_versions.check_id` is `ondelete=CASCADE`, so deleting a check (or a suite, which cascades to its checks) wipes its entire `check_versions` history. History survives *edits* (SCD Type 4) but not *deletion*.
2. **No general audit log.** `connections` (credential/config changes), `shares` (grant/revoke), `trigger_bindings` are SCD Type 1 (overwrite + `updated_at`) or hard-deleted with no who/when/before/after trail.
3. **All deletes are hard deletes** (`session.delete`) — no soft-delete (`deleted_at`) anywhere. A deleted connection orphans the meaning of past runs ("what did this run actually check?").
4. **No SCD Type 2** (`valid_from`/`valid_to` versioned dimensions) anywhere.

## Decision needed (ADR)

Pick the history/audit posture for v1.x+:
- **(a)** Preserve check history on delete — `check_versions.check_id` → `RESTRICT`/`SET NULL` + self-contained identity, or a tombstone.
- **(b)** Soft-delete (`deleted_at`) for `connections`/`suites` so run lineage survives.
- **(c)** A single cross-entity **audit log** (`actor, entity_type, entity_id, action, before, after, ts`) — cheaper/uniform vs per-table versioning; covers connections/shares/triggers that have no history today.
- **(d)** Full SCD Type 2 on selected dimensions (heaviest — see the cost analysis on this issue).

## Acceptance
- [ ] ADR recording the chosen posture + rationale + which entities get which treatment
- [ ] Follow-up implementation issue(s) per the decision (e.g. the `check_versions` ondelete fix is small and could be pulled forward)

## Context
From the history/SCD review. Single-tenant v1 likely doesn't need full SCD2, but the check-history-on-delete (1) is a near-term correctness item worth deciding deliberately.


## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] ADR merged deciding the history/audit remainder: cross-entity audit log + soft-delete — accepted or explicitly re-deferred with rationale
- [ ] Consistent with the #596 G-d design and #431; follow-up issues filed if accepted

_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

FIRST read: CLAUDE.md (root), CONTRIBUTING.md, `gh issue view 595`, docs/perf-baseline.md, and `gh issue view 755` (OOM → silent 60-min hang, the evidence for the guardrail). input.description: #327 profiler query batching
input.prompt:
You are implementing GitHub issue #327 in the DataQ repo (TheurgicDuke771/DataQ). You are in an isolated git worktree of /Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ — work there, branch off main as `perf/issue-327-profiler-batch-topvalues`.

FIRST read: CLAUDE.md (root), CONTRIBUTING.md, `gh issue view 327`. Then the code: backend/app/services/profile_service.py (`profile_table` — 1 aggregate query + one top-values query per column in a Python loop), backend/app/datasources/sql.py (shared SQL-identifier allowlist), and how the profiler's queries are built/executed per datasource (SQLAlchemy Core builders — note #937: quoting must come from the CONNECTION's dialect, never hand-rolled; UC uses backticks, Snowflake double-quotes).

SCOPE: collapse the N+1 per-column top-values round-trips into O(1)–O(2) batched queries per table (e.g. UNION ALL of per-column grouped+limited subqueries, with each value projected as a CAST to a common type or per-column marker columns — the issue warns mixed-type `value` projection coerces per-dialect). Requirements:
- Build with SQLAlchemy Core so each dialect quotes/renders itself; NO hand-rolled quoting, no f-string SQL.

LIMIT chunk_size)`, each batch individually committed, until an affected count `< chunk_size`. `purge_expired_sample_failures` gained an optional `chunk_size` kwarg threaded through to both column sweeps.

**Tests:** `backend/tests/services/test_run_retention.py` — 14/14 pass (11 existing + 3 new batching regression tests). The new `test_batch_count_matches_the_configured_chunk_size` was mutation-verified: reverting `_purge_column` to the old single-UPDATE shape makes it fail correctly (2 UPDATEs issued instead of 4), while the other two new tests pass under both shapes by design (documented in their docstrings — they prove correctness, not batching per se). Full backend suite: 3936 passed, 1 skipped, 97.17% coverage. `black --check`, `ruff check`, `mypy`, `bandit` all clean. Migration tested `alembic upgrade head` → `downgrade -1` → `upgrade head` against a real throwaway scratch Postgres database (dropped after use).</result>

LIMIT chunk_size)`, each batch individually committed, until an affected count `< chunk_size`. `purge_expired_sample_failures` gained an optional `chunk_size` kwarg threaded through to both column sweeps.

<note>A task-notification fires each time this agent stops with no live background children of its own. The user can send it another message and resume it, so the same task-id may notify more than once.</note>
<result>Reviewed the diff, migration, and `run_service.py` 1276–1465 in the worktree. All the flagged efficiency problems are real and verifiable from the code. Six findings, ordered by severity.

## Finding 1 — Index docstring claim is false: the partial index retains every passing-check row forever

**File:** `backend/alembic/versions/fbf4fe92e295_add_results_unpurged_created_index.py` lines 20–26 (same claim repeated in `backend/app/db/models.py` lines 862–866, "small, shrinking working set")

**Summary:** "the index only ever covers the sweep's actual working set, not the whole table" does not hold — the index asymptotically covers ~the whole table.

**Failure scenario:** A row leaves the partial index only when `sample_failures_purged_at` is stamped. But the first purge half's `jsonb_typeof(sample_failures) IS NOT NULL AND != 'null'` guard (run_service.py:1427–1429) permanently excludes every row whose `sample_failures` is SQL NULL — i.e. **every passing check's result, the majority of the table** — so those rows are never stamped and never leave the index. The index therefore grows linearly with total results written, dominated by never-eligible entries. Concretely: every daily sweep's index range scan (`created_at < cutoff` covers all history) must heap-fetch every one of those dead entries to evaluate the typeof guards (typeof can't be answered from an index storing only `created_at`), so the daily sweep is O(all historical passing rows) every day — not O(the day's expired crop) as the migration claims. The index only excludes already-purged rows, the *minority* on a passing-dominated table, so the headline perf claim of the PR largely evaporates.

**Fix:** put the typeof guards into the index predicate — `WHERE sample_failures_purged_at IS NULL AND sample_failures IS NOT NULL AND jsonb_typeof(sample_failures) <> 'null'` — which the sweep's predicate still implies. Then never-eligible rows never enter the index, and it genuinely shrinks to the working set.

## Finding 2 — Batched loop re-scans the ever-growing dead prefix per chunk: catch-up is superlinear

**File:** `backend/app/services/run_service.py` lines 1329–1347

**Summary:** Each chunk's `SELECT id ... LIMIT chunk_size` restarts the index scan from the bottom of the `created_at` range, re-skipping all never-eligible entries every iteration — no keyset progression.

**Failure scenario:** Never-eligible (passing-row) entries below cutoff don't shrink between iterations (Finding 1), and eligible entries interleave with them by `created_at`. Chunk *k* must skip past roughly `k·chunk_size·(P/E)` dead entries (P = never-eligible rows below cutoff, E = eligible backlog) before assembling its 500 IDs, each skip a heap fetch to evaluate the typeof filter. Summed over `B = E/500` chunks that is **~P·E/1000 heap fetches**. Concrete: P = 2M passing rows, E = 100k backlog → ~2×10⁸ row visits across 200 chunks, versus the pre-PR single seq scan visiting ~2.1M rows once — the "catch-up run … which is precisely the case the AC's 'no lock-contention regression' check targets" (comment at 1281–1284) is exactly the case this makes ~100× *worse* in total I/O. Fixing the index predicate (Finding 1) collapses this, since purged rows then leave the index and each rescan starts at the first live entry; keyset pagination (`ORDER BY created_at, id` + resume-after cursor) is the belt-and-braces alternative.

## Finding 3 — The observed_value half cannot use the new index at all; batching turned 1 full scan into N full scans

**File:** `backend/app/services/run_service.py` lines 1438–1445

**Summary:** The second half's predicate (`created_at < cutoff AND jsonb_typeof(observed_value->'observed_value') = 'array'`) has no `sample_failures_purged_at IS NULL` term, so it does not imply the partial index's predicate — Postgres will never use `ix_results_unpurged_created` for it. There is no other `created_at` index.

**Failure scenario:** Every chunk of the observed_value half is a sequential scan (LIMIT lets early chunks stop early, but the final iteration — which always runs, that's the loop's exit condition — scans the entire table). For an observed_value catch-up backlog of E rows, the pre-PR code did exactly **one** full scan; this PR does up to **⌈E/500⌉ + 1** full scans. The PR regressed the very half it claims to have indexed. Fix: a second partial index `ON results (created_at) WHERE jsonb_typeof(observed_value->'observed_value') = 'array'` — small by construction (only set-oriented expectations produce the array shape) and exactly implied by this half's predicate.

## Finding 4 — `_purge_column` docstring's "index makes the extra scan pass cheap" is a broken perf claim

**File:** `backend/app/services/run_service.py` lines 1313–1314

**Summary:** The justification for keeping two separate UPDATEs ("The daily 01:17 UTC cadence and the `ix_results_unpurged_created` partial index (#323) make the extra scan pass cheap") is false for one of the two passes.

**Failure scenario:** The "extra scan pass" being excused is precisely the observed_value UPDATE — the one that cannot use the index (Finding 3) and seq-scans daily. The rationale recorded in the code for an architectural choice (two UPDATEs vs one CASE-based UPDATE) rests on an index benefit that doesn't exist for that pass; the next person reading this will wrongly believe both halves are indexed. Either add the second partial index or correct the claim.

## Finding 5 — Extra empty round-trip when backlog is an exact multiple of chunk_size

**File:** `backend/app/services/run_service.py` lines 1342–1346

**Summary:** Exit sentinel is `affected < chunk_size`, so a backlog of exactly `k·chunk_size` runs one additional iteration that selects and updates nothing.

**Failure scenario:** The wasted iteration is not just a round-trip: for the observed_value half it is **one additional full sequential scan of `results`** (Finding 3), and for the sample_failures half one additional full walk of the dead index prefix (Finding 2) — the emptiest iteration is the most expensive one, because finding zero matching rows means exhausting the entire candidate range. Also note the loop *always* runs at least once even when nothing is eligible (steady state for the observed_value half most days is 0 rows → a daily full seq scan to conclude "nothing to do" — pre-existing shape, but the PR's docstrings now describe it as cheap). Cheap mitigation for the multiple-of-chunk case: run the SELECT first and skip the UPDATE when it returns no IDs, or exit on `affected == 0` after a `chunk_size`-sized batch only when a follow-up probe is free — but the real fix is the indexes above, which make the empty pass cheap for real.

## Finding 6 — The new index disables HOT updates for the purge and taxes every result insert

**File:** `backend/alembic/versions/fbf4fe92e295_add_results_unpurged_created_index.py` line 70–71 (index definition)

**Summary:** Two standing costs the migration docstring doesn't account: (a) `sample_failures_purged_at` now appears in an index *predicate*, so every purge UPDATE is HOT-disqualified; (b) every result INSERT (all new rows have `purged_at` NULL) must add an entry to this index.

**Failure scenario:** (a) Before this PR no index referenced `sample_failures` or `sample_failures_purged_at`, so purge UPDATEs could be HOT — heap-only, no index maintenance. Now each purged row writes new index tuples into `ix_results_run_id`, `ix_results_check_id`, and the new index, tripling per-row write amplification on exactly the bulk operation the PR set out to lighten. (b) The insert-path tax funds an index whose entries, per Finding 1, mostly never earn their keep (never-eligible passing rows sit in it forever). Both costs become acceptable — small index, few entries — once the typeof guards move into the index predicate (Finding 1's fix), because then passing-row inserts skip the index entirely and only sample-bearing rows pay. As shipped, the hottest write path in the system (`results` insert, one per check per run) pays for an index that doesn't deliver its claimed benefit.

---

**Bottom line for the PR's perf claims:** the batching-for-lock-bounding part is sound in shape, but the index as specified doesn't deliver the claimed working-set bound (Finding 1), the chunk loop makes catch-up sweeps asymptotically *worse* than the single UPDATE it replaced (Findings 2, 3), and the second purge half is entirely unindexed despite docstrings implying otherwise (Findings 3, 4). The coherent fix is one index-predicate change plus one additional partial index; both are implied by the sweeps' own WHERE clauses and require no code change in `_purge_column`.</result>

<result>I've read every hunk, the enclosing functions, the migration, the model, the tests, the `db_session` fixture, and the worker caller. Here are my candidate findings.

## Findings

### 1. `chunk_size=0` makes `_purge_column` spin forever (infinite loop, no guard)
- **File:** `backend/app/services/run_service.py`, **line:** 1345 (`if affected < chunk_size:`; param at 1296/1355)
- **Summary:** With `chunk_size=0` the exit condition `affected < chunk_size` can never be true, so the `while True` loop never terminates.
- **Failure scenario:** `purge_expired_sample_failures(session, retention_days=30, chunk_size=0)` — `LIMIT 0` selects zero rows → `affected = 0` → `0 < 0` is False → the loop hot-spins issuing empty UPDATE + `commit()` forever, permanently occupying a Celery worker slot (the beat task never returns; next day's beat stacks another). A negative `chunk_size` fails loud instead (Postgres `ERROR: LIMIT must not be negative`), but `0` is a silent hang. `chunk_size` is a public keyword on both functions with no `<= 0` validation and no test for it. One-line guard (`if chunk_size <= 0: raise ValueError` or clamp) fixes it.

### 2. Guard predicates were moved out of the UPDATE's WHERE — concurrent sweeps can re-purge/re-stamp already-purged rows (READ COMMITTED / EvalPlanQual regression)
- **File:** `backend/app/services/run_service.py`, **line:** 1337 (`.where(Result.id.in_(candidate_chunk))`)

## Findings

**1. The observed_value half cannot use the new partial index — and chunking multiplies its full scans (perf regression inside a perf PR).**
- File: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`, line 1439-1445 (second `_purge_column` call); also the migration docstring at `backend/alembic/versions/fbf4fe92e295_add_results_unpurged_created_index.py` lines 26-32.
- The index is `ON results (created_at) WHERE sample_failures_purged_at IS NULL`. The observed_value sweep's predicate is `created_at < cutoff AND jsonb_typeof(observed_value->'observed_value') = 'array'` — it does not constrain `sample_failures_purged_at`, so its predicate does not imply the index's WHERE and Postgres **cannot** use the partial index for it (rows with array-shaped `observed_value` legitimately exist with `purged_at` non-NULL, e.g. sample purged earlier or never present).
- Failure scenario: a catch-up backlog of M eligible observed_value rows now costs `ceil(M/500)+1` sequential scans of the unbounded table (each chunk's `SELECT id ... LIMIT 500` subquery restarts the scan; previously-purged rows no longer match, so every scan re-reads the prefix), versus exactly **one** scan pre-PR. The daily steady-state zero-match iteration also remains one full seq scan the new index does nothing for. The old single-UPDATE shape was strictly better for this half; the batching should either be index-supported (e.g. a second partial index on the array predicate) or the docstring claims scoped to the sample half.

**2. Atomicity loss → permanent undercount in the audit log / return value.**
- File: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`, line 1343 (`session.commit()` per chunk) vs. the log emission at line 1455.
- Old invariant: one transaction covering both purges + a log line whose counts exactly equaled the durable effect — a failure meant zero rows purged and a complete retry next day. New: an exception or worker death at chunk k leaves chunks 1..k-1 durably purged, the `sample_failures_purged` event never fires, and the task returns nothing. Because purged rows self-exclude (`purged_at` stamped / column nulled), the **next** sweep's counts exclude them too — so those rows never appear in any log event, ever.
- Failure scenario: anything keying off this event's `purged`/`total_purged` (the docstring at 1451-1454 explicitly protects such consumers) permanently under-reports after any mid-sweep failure; a PII-audit reconciling "rows scrubbed" against log history now has an unexplainable gap. Not re-established anywhere in the new code; at minimum a per-chunk progress log (or logging inside `_purge_column`) would restore accounting.

**3. Cross-column consistency window between the two halves.**
- File: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`, lines 1423-1445.
- Old: both column purges became visible atomically at the caller's single commit. New: half 1's chunks commit while half 2 hasn't run; a worker death between the calls leaves rows `sample_failures`-purged but with the PII-bearing `observed_value` array intact until the next beat (~25h extra exposure of exactly the data the sweep exists to remove — and half 2 is the slow, index-less half per finding 1, widening the window). Readers meanwhile see the intermediate state; mitigated for *display* by #1115's read-time "partial" redaction state, but the PII-retention SLA half-miss is real and unlogged (finding 2 compounds it).

**4. A helper now commits a caller-owned session — contract change invisible in the signature.**
- File: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`, line 1343.
- Old: `_purge_column` was pure DML; the sole commit was the caller's, so a caller could compose the purge into a larger transaction and roll everything back. New: the loop unconditionally commits at least once (even a zero-affected first iteration), flushing **any** pending caller state at the first chunk boundary. Current callers are safe (beat task = fresh session; tests = savepoint fixture), so this is latent, but the failure scenario is nameable: a future caller that writes its own row (audit entry, admin-triggered purge record) before calling `purge_expired_sample_failures` has that write committed mid-helper, and its later `rollback()` becomes a silent no-op. Also asymmetric: the `retention_days <= 0` path (line 1417) returns without committing, so "this function commits" is now true on one path and false on another. Deserves at least a docstring warning on `purge_expired_sample_failures` that the session is committed as a side effect (the current docstring says "individually-committed batches" only via reference to `_purge_column`).

**5. `affected < chunk_size` sentinel can terminate the sweep early under concurrent row deletion.**
- File: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`, line 1345.
- The old single UPDATE evaluated the predicate once and touched every matching row regardless of concurrent activity. The new loop treats `rowcount < chunk_size` as "candidate set exhausted" — but `rowcount` counts rows actually updated, and results rows **are** row-deleted in prod via the suite-delete FK cascade (#540/#542). Under READ COMMITTED, if a concurrent suite delete commits while a chunk's UPDATE runs, EvalPlanQual skips the deleted rows, so the subquery can select 500 ids while the UPDATE reports, say, 480 — the loop breaks with eligible rows still beyond the LIMIT.
- Failure scenario: a suite deletion concurrent with a catch-up sweep silently truncates that day's purge; expired PII survives an extra day, and (per finding 2's shape) nothing logs that the sweep stopped early. Self-heals next day, so severity is low, but the sentinel would be robust as `if affected == 0: break` (termination still guaranteed by the monotonic self-exclusion the docstring itself relies on) at the cost of one extra empty iteration.

**6. Deleted docstring claim — verified, disposition recorded.**
- File: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`, old lines 1149-1150 of the diff ("indexed `created_at` cutoff make the extra scan pass cheap").
- The deleted claim was **false when written** — no `created_at` index existed pre-PR (only `ix_results_run_id`/`ix_results_check_id`), so the "extra scan pass" the #1253 two-UPDATE design was costed against was two full seq scans, not two index scans. The PR corrects this, so the deletion itself is verified-benign. However, the *replacement* text (lines 1315-1316: "the `ix_results_unpurged_created` partial index (#323) make the extra scan pass cheap") re-establishes the claim only for the `sample_failures` half — for the `observed_value` half it is exactly as false as its predecessor, per finding 1. Same overclaim in the migration docstring ("matches the sweep's two most selective predicates" — true of one of the sweep's two queries).

**Checked and clean (no finding):** the migration chains correctly off head `5ffa2405f9e8`; the model-side `Index(..., postgresql_where=...)` keeps `create_all` test DBs schema-equal to migrated ones; both halves' `values` provably self-exclude from their `extra_where` so the loop terminates; the fixed `moment`/`cutoff` means wall-clock advance cannot make new rows eligible mid-sweep; the test fixture's savepoint mode absorbs the in-helper commits; and `test_batch_count_matches_the_configured_chunk_size`'s expected count of 4 UPDATEs (3+3+1 sample, 1 empty observed) is arithmetically right.

Highest-priority items: findings 1 and 2; finding 5 is the one with a concrete prod trigger (suite delete during catch-up).</result>

`backend/alembic/versions/fbf4fe92e295_...py:76` with `backend/alembic/env.py` (`_MIGRATION_LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS = 15_000`, set engine-wide via connect `options`). CIC's two wait phases (waiting out every transaction holding a snapshot on `results`) are ordinary lock waits, which `lock_timeout` cancels. The migrate job deliberately runs *before* the api/worker roll while the old beat and in-flight GX runs are still writing (env.py's own comment says so). Failure scenario: a result-inserting transaction outlasts 15s during CIC's wait → statement cancelled → deploy fails **and** an INVALID `ix_results_unpurged_created` is left behind; the deploy retry re-runs the migration, `IF NOT EXISTS` matches the (invalid) name, silently no-ops, and stamps the revision applied. The sample half stamps `sample_failures_purged_at` only where `jsonb_typeof(sample_failures)` is non-NULL and != 'null' (`run_service.py:1427-1429`). A result whose `sample_failures` is SQL NULL — i.e. every check that recorded no failing samples, the large majority of rows — is never stamped, so it satisfies `WHERE sample_failures_purged_at IS NULL` permanently. The index therefore grows roughly with total results, not with the sweep's working set, contradicting the migration's stated size rationale ("once a row is purged it drops out of the index permanently … only ever covers the sweep's actual working set"). Failure scenario: after months of accumulation, each daily sweep's first chunk subquery index-scans `created_at < cutoff` through all historical never-sampled entries (heap-fetching each to fail the typeof filter) before finding its 500 matches — per-chunk cost trends back toward the pre-PR scan. Fix: stamp `sample_failures_purged_at` unconditionally for rows past cutoff (dropping the typeof guards from `extra_where`; NULL→NULL is harmless, though the per-column rowcount telemetry would need rethinking), or fold the typeof conditions into the index predicate.

**4. [run_service.py:1447-1463, minor] Mid-sweep failure now leaves committed purges with no `sample_failures_purged` log event**
Pre-PR, one transaction meant log-absence matched data-absence: a failed sweep rolled everything back. Now `_purge_column` commits per chunk, but the `sample_failures_purged` structured event (line 1455) is only emitted after both halves complete. Failure scenario: a catch-up sweep dies at chunk 40 — ~20k rows are scrubbed and durably committed, the task raises, and no purge event fires; anything keyed off that event's counts (the docstring explicitly calls out alert/dashboard consumers of this event's shape) silently undercounts, and the next day's event reports only the remainder, so the audit trail can never account for the committed rows. Consider logging per-chunk or in a try/finally with running totals.

Findings 1-3 have concrete, nameable failure scenarios and are worth carrying to the PR; finding 4 is minor but real. No call site is broken by the signature changes or the mid-call commits themselves.</result>

**4. [run_service.py:1447-1463, minor] Mid-sweep failure now leaves committed purges with no `sample_failures_purged` log event**
Pre-PR, one transaction meant log-absence matched data-absence: a failed sweep rolled everything back. Consider logging per-chunk or in a try/finally with running totals.

content.text:
All eight finders are in. The angles converge strongly — six of eight independently found the same top defect. Consolidated verdict:

**Must-fix (multi-angle confirmed):**
1. The `observed_value` purge half can't use the new partial index (its predicate doesn't imply the index WHERE) — and chunking turned its catch-up from 1 full scan into ⌈N/500⌉ full scans. Needs a second partial index on the array predicate.
2. The index's "shrinking working set" claim is false — passing-check rows (the majority) never get stamped, never leave the index. The typeof guards belong in the index predicate.
3. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS` + env.py's 15s `lock_timeout` → a cancelled CIC leaves an INVALID index that the retry silently accepts and stamps. Needs `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS` first for self-healing.
4. Loop exit `affected < chunk_size`: `chunk_size=0` hot-spins forever, and concurrent suite-delete cascades (EPQ row skips) cause silent early exit stranding PII backlog. Exit on `affected == 0`.
5. EPQ re-stamp race: guards moved into the subquery only — repeat them on the outer UPDATE.
6. Chunked-DML loop is a second diverged copy of `asset_service`'s (dropped `rowcount or 0`) — extract the shared helper.

**Minor:** per-chunk/finally logging for the undercount-on-failure gap, `ORDER BY created_at`, `perf:` title not in the repo's closed commit-type vocabulary, dead trailing commit, one redundant test; plus one to file (parity test can't see literal-free predicate inversions).

**F2 — "small, shrinking working set" is false: passing-check rows never leave the index.** The sweep stamps `sample_failures_purged_at` only where `jsonb_typeof(sample_failures)` is non-NULL and ≠ 'null'; rows with SQL-NULL `sample_failures` — every passing check, the majority of the table — stay in `WHERE sample_failures_purged_at IS NULL` forever. The index grows ~linearly with the table; each daily sweep heap-fetches the entire dead prefix to fail the typeof filter, and each chunk re-scans it (superlinear catch-up). It also taxes every result INSERT and HOT-disqualifies purge UPDATEs for entries that never earn their keep. **Fix:** fold the typeof guards into the index predicate (`WHERE sample_failures_purged_at IS NULL AND sample_failures IS NOT NULL AND jsonb_typeof(sample_failures) <> 'null'`), keeping the sweep's WHERE textually matching so the planner proves implication. Verify with `EXPLAIN` on a seeded table that **both** halves hit their indexes, and re-run the before/after numbers.

**F3 — CIC retry trap: a cancelled `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` leaves an INVALID index that `IF NOT EXISTS` silently accepts.** `alembic/env.py` sets `lock_timeout=15s` engine-wide, and CIC's wait phases are ordinary lock waits — the migrate job runs while the old revision's beat/GX runs still write `results`, so a >15s writer cancels the CIC. Retry then no-ops on the INVALID index and stamps head; prod permanently carries an index the planner never uses, with zero signal. **Fix:** `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS` immediately before each CREATE inside the same `autocommit_block()` (self-healing retry), for both indexes.

**F4 — loop exit `affected < chunk_size` has two failure modes.** (a) `chunk_size=0` (public kwarg, unvalidated): `LIMIT 0` → `affected=0` → `0 < 0` False → infinite empty UPDATE+commit loop occupying the worker slot. (b) Concurrent suite-delete FK-cascades (#540/#542) delete selected rows mid-chunk; EPQ skips them, `affected = 500−k < 500`, loop breaks with the remaining backlog stranded until tomorrow, unlogged. **Fix:** exit on `affected == 0` (termination stays guaranteed by monotonic self-exclusion; costs one empty iteration — cheap once F1/F2 land) + a `chunk_size >= 1` guard.

## Batching design — and how mixed types are handled

**A rank driver LEFT-joined to one derived table per column**, not a `UNION ALL`:

```sql
SELECT r.rn, t0.value AS v_0, t0.freq AS f_0, t1.value AS v_1, t1.freq AS f_1, …
FROM (SELECT 1 AS rn UNION ALL SELECT 2 AS rn …) AS dq_ranks r
LEFT JOIN (SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY count(*) DESC, c0) AS rn,
                  c0 AS value, count(*) AS freq
           FROM tbl WHERE c0 IS NOT NULL GROUP BY c0
           ORDER BY count(*) DESC, c0 LIMIT n) AS dq_top_0 ON dq_top_0.rn = r.rn
LEFT JOIN (…) AS dq_top_1 ON dq_top_1.rn = r.rn
ORDER BY r.rn
```

Each derived table is *exactly* the query `build_top_values_query` already built, plus a `ROW_NUMBER()` on the same ordering expression — which is both the join key and what restores per-column order (ties included) without re-sorting values in Python, where string collation wouldn't match the warehouse's. All SQLAlchemy Core; the connection's dialect quotes everything.

**Mixed types are handled by never unifying them** — each column keeps its own output column and its own type, so NUMERIC arrives as `Decimal` and TIMESTAMP as a datetime.

**The `UNION ALL` shape was built first and is the trap the issue flagged.** A union unifies branch types, so all values land in one `value` projection (Postgres refuses `integer`/`text`; Snowflake silently coerces to `VARCHAR`). Per-column value slots padded with `NULL` **do not rescue it**: an untyped `NULL` resolves pairwise left-to-right, so in a left-deep union tree two padding slots settle on `text` before the branch owning the slot is reached — Postgres rejected it with `UNION types text and timestamp without time zone cannot be matched`. It compiled cleanly and passed every SQL-text assertion; only running it found it.

Chunk size `_TOP_VALUES_BATCH = 25` is **measured**: on 50 cols × 50k rows the pass held ~270 ms at every chunk from 8–25 and jumped to ~820 ms as a single 50-way join (Postgres switches to its genetic optimiser at 12 relations). 25 puts the endpoint's own 50-column cap at exactly 2 batched round-trips.

## Fallback semantics

Any exception from a batch → the whole set is re-collected column-by-column via `_top_values_per_column` (kept as live code), logging `profile_top_values_batch_fallback` with the exception type so a perpetually-falling-back warehouse is visible rather than merely slow. A `DataQError` (bad identifier) is re-raised untouched, not retried. `top_n < 1` routes directly to the per-column path; an empty column list issues nothing. If the retry also fails, the pre-existing 502 is unchanged.

## Before/after (real seams, seeded local Postgres, 50k rows, top_n=10)

| columns | round-trips | local median | +50 ms/RT | +250 ms/RT | +1000 ms/RT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 | 30 → **2** | 152 → 140 ms | 1.98 → **0.28 s** | 7.99 → **0.69 s** | 30.51 → **2.16 s** (14.1×) |
| 40 | 40 → **2** | 193 → 189 ms | 2.67 → **0.31 s** | 10.54 → **0.70 s** | 40.46 → **2.25 s** (18.0×) |
| 50 | 50 → **2** | 276 → 263 ms | 3.34 → **0.39 s** | 13.46 → **0.81 s** | 50.85 → **2.27 s** (22.4×) |

Every run asserted `batched == per-column` before timing.

## Tests

- **New live-Postgres module** (`test_profile_batched_top_values_pg.py`, skips without `TEST_DATABASE_URL`): asserts **equivalence, not plausibility** — batched vs per-column equal in values *and* `type()` (so `10.5` can't pass for `Decimal('10.50')`), count tie-break, per-column `top_n`, native NUMERIC/TIMESTAMP, short-column LEFT-JOIN padding, all-null columns, and an identical end-to-end `ProfileResult` on batched vs forced-fallback. Adversarial-but-legal names: `Status`, `ORDER_TS`, `amount$usd`.
- **Unit tests**: SQL shape, rank driver, fragment-equivalence with the per-column builder, mixed-case quoting, 3-part UC namespace, injection-shaped identifiers, both guard rails, collector behaviour.
- **Endpoint tests**: round-trip count (12 cols → 2 executes), chunking arithmetic, fallback path.
- **Found and fixed a silent coverage hole**: `_FakeConn` understood only the old shape, so every endpoint test was passing *through the fallback* — green while covering a path production doesn't take.
- **Mutation-checked: 10/10 mutations killed** (dropped rn sort, dropped tie-break, no fallback, never batch, padding-as-data, ignored chunk size, no outer ORDER BY, rank from 0, INNER join, dropped IS NOT NULL).
- Local battery: Black/Ruff/mypy/Bandit + **3955 passed, 1 skipped, 97.18% coverage**.

## ⚠️ Pending live verification (stated in the PR body, progress.md and CLAUDE.md)

Per the **#953 rule**, the batched SQL is **proven on PostgreSQL only**. Snowflake and Unity Catalog acceptance is **NOT proven and not claimed** — `ORDER BY … LIMIT` in a derived table, `ROW_NUMBER()` over an aggregate and chained LEFT JOINs are standard and expected to work, but the union design in this same PR compiled cleanly and was refused by an engine. **Live Snowflake + Unity Catalog verification is yours to run before #327 is considered fully verified.** Until then the fallback is the safety net: worst case is current performance, not a broken profiler.</result>

<result>**PR: [#1323](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1323)** — `perf: batch the profiler's N+1 per-column top-values queries (#327)`, open, `Fixes #327`, milestone set, full CI green (17/17), not merged, no `/code-review` run.

## Batching design — and how mixed types are handled

**A rank driver LEFT-joined to one derived table per column**, not a `UNION ALL`:

```sql
SELECT r.rn, t0.value AS v_0, t0.freq AS f_0, t1.value AS v_1, t1.freq AS f_1, …
FROM (SELECT 1 AS rn UNION ALL SELECT 2 AS rn …) AS dq_ranks r
LEFT JOIN (SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY count(*) DESC, c0) AS rn,
                  c0 AS value, count(*) AS freq
           FROM tbl WHERE c0 IS NOT NULL GROUP BY c0
           ORDER BY count(*) DESC, c0 LIMIT n) AS dq_top_0 ON dq_top_0.rn = r.rn
LEFT JOIN (…) AS dq_top_1 ON dq_top_1.rn = r.rn
ORDER BY r.rn
```

Each derived table is *exactly* the query `build_top_values_query` already built, plus a `ROW_NUMBER()` on the same ordering expression — which is both the join key and what restores per-column order (ties included) without re-sorting values in Python, where string collation wouldn't match the warehouse's. All SQLAlchemy Core; the connection's dialect quotes everything.

**Mixed types are handled by never unifying them** — each column keeps its own output column and its own type, so NUMERIC arrives as `Decimal` and TIMESTAMP as a datetime.

**The `UNION ALL` shape was built first and is the trap the issue flagged.** A union unifies branch types, so all values land in one `value` projection (Postgres refuses `integer`/`text`; Snowflake silently coerces to `VARCHAR`). Per-column value slots padded with `NULL` **do not rescue it**: an untyped `NULL` resolves pairwise left-to-right, so in a left-deep union tree two padding slots settle on `text` before the branch owning the slot is reached — Postgres rejected it with `UNION types text and timestamp without time zone cannot be matched`. It compiled cleanly and passed every SQL-text assertion; only running it found it.

Chunk size `_TOP_VALUES_BATCH = 25` is **measured**: on 50 cols × 50k rows the pass held ~270 ms at every chunk from 8–25 and jumped to ~820 ms as a single 50-way join (Postgres switches to its genetic optimiser at 12 relations). 25 puts the endpoint's own 50-column cap at exactly 2 batched round-trips.

## Fallback semantics

Any exception from a batch → the whole set is re-collected column-by-column via `_top_values_per_column` (kept as live code), logging `profile_top_values_batch_fallback` with the exception type so a perpetually-falling-back warehouse is visible rather than merely slow. A `DataQError` (bad identifier) is re-raised untouched, not retried. `top_n < 1` routes directly to the per-column path; an empty column list issues nothing. If the retry also fails, the pre-existing 502 is unchanged.

## Before/after (real seams, seeded local Postgres, 50k rows, top_n=10)

| columns | round-trips | local median | +50 ms/RT | +250 ms/RT | +1000 ms/RT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 | 30 → **2** | 152 → 140 ms | 1.98 → **0.28 s** | 7.99 → **0.69 s** | 30.51 → **2.16 s** (14.1×) |
| 40 | 40 → **2** | 193 → 189 ms | 2.67 → **0.31 s** | 10.54 → **0.70 s** | 40.46 → **2.25 s** (18.0×) |
| 50 | 50 → **2** | 276 → 263 ms | 3.34 → **0.39 s** | 13.46 → **0.81 s** | 50.85 → **2.27 s** (22.4×) |

Every run asserted `batched == per-column` before timing.

## Tests

- **New live-Postgres module** (`test_profile_batched_top_values_pg.py`, skips without `TEST_DATABASE_URL`): asserts **equivalence, not plausibility** — batched vs per-column equal in values *and* `type()` (so `10.5` can't pass for `Decimal('10.50')`), count tie-break, per-column `top_n`, native NUMERIC/TIMESTAMP, short-column LEFT-JOIN padding, all-null columns, and an identical end-to-end `ProfileResult` on batched vs forced-fallback. Adversarial-but-legal names: `Status`, `ORDER_TS`, `amount$usd`.
- **Unit tests**: SQL shape, rank driver, fragment-equivalence with the per-column builder, mixed-case quoting, 3-part UC namespace, injection-shaped identifiers, both guard rails, collector behaviour.
- **Endpoint tests**: round-trip count (12 cols → 2 executes), chunking arithmetic, fallback path.
- **Found and fixed a silent coverage hole**: `_FakeConn` understood only the old shape, so every endpoint test was passing *through the fallback* — green while covering a path production doesn't take.
- **Mutation-checked: 10/10 mutations killed** (dropped rn sort, dropped tie-break, no fallback, never batch, padding-as-data, ignored chunk size, no outer ORDER BY, rank from 0, INNER join, dropped IS NOT NULL).
- Local battery: Black/Ruff/mypy/Bandit + **3955 passed, 1 skipped, 97.18% coverage**.

## ⚠️ Pending live verification (stated in the PR body, progress.md and CLAUDE.md)

Per the **#953 rule**, the batched SQL is **proven on PostgreSQL only**. Snowflake and Unity Catalog acceptance is **NOT proven and not claimed** — `ORDER BY … LIMIT` in a derived table, `ROW_NUMBER()` over an aggregate and chained LEFT JOINs are standard and expected to work, but the union design in this same PR compiled cleanly and was refused by an engine. **Live Snowflake + Unity Catalog verification is yours to run before #327 is considered fully verified.** Until then the fallback is the safety net: worst case is current performance, not a broken profiler.</result>

## PR

**#1325** — https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1325
`feat: scale-aware execution — sampling + partition batching + OOM guardrail for flat-file/UC runners (#595)` · `Fixes #595` · milestone *v1.1 Week 6* · 8 commits · **all 16 CI checks pass** on head `56b3e311`.

## Design choices

**Where the spec lives** — on the suite's run-target JSONB (`{"sampling": {"strategy": "head"|"random", "rows": N, "seed": ?}}`), so no migration for the config side. `SampleSpec` sits in `datasources/base.py` beside `BatchSpec`; behaviour is a new pure module `datasources/sampling.py` (100% covered).

**Where sampled-ness is stored** — new nullable `results.sampling` JSONB (migration `4d23b47ee564`, up/down tested against Postgres), returned by `GET /runs/{id}` unredacted (it carries counts, not target data). **Per-result, not per-run**: within one run a volume monitor pushes down (exact) while the expectations beside it saw 100k of 5M — a run-level flag would have to lie about one. `sampled` is stored explicitly, so a "sample" larger than the dataset reports as the complete read it is instead of crying wolf on every small target. `null` = complete read, which is also what every pre-existing row means — no backfill.

**Caps** — `RUN_MAX_SCAN_BYTES` (128 MiB, flat files) and `RUN_MAX_SCAN_ROWS` (1.5M, UC). `0` disables the cap *and* its probe. Sampling **replaces** the cap rather than stacking with it.

**What UC pushes down** — freshness/volume were already scalar SQL aggregates and `schema_drift` already read `information_schema` (verified, unchanged). The gap was the *expectation* read: now `LIMIT rows+1` (head) or `TABLESAMPLE (p PERCENT) … LIMIT rows` sized from `COUNT(*)` (random). Not `ORDER BY rand()` (global sort) and not `TABLESAMPLE (n ROWS)` (Spark implements it as a plain LIMIT — a head sample wearing a random label).

Sampling is **refused at save time** on Snowflake/Iceberg rather than ignored, and never applied to freshness (a MAX over a sample is a *smaller* maximum → healthy data reported critically stale).

## Measurements (docs/perf-baseline.md §W6)

5M-row order-lines, real runner, five expectations. Floor 329 MiB.

| Object | Mode | Outcome | Wall | Peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CSV 249 MB | full, cap off | 5/5 pass | 4.26 s | **2,210 MiB** |
| CSV 249 MB | full, cap on | **refused** | **0.00 s** | 329 MiB |
| CSV 249 MB | head 100k | 5/5, `sampled: true` | 0.15 s | **411 MiB** |
| CSV 249 MB | random 100k | 5/5, `sampled: true` | 1.98 s | **550 MiB** |
| Parquet 114 MB | full, cap off | 5/5 pass | 2.11 s | 1,290 MiB |
| Parquet 114 MB | head/random 100k | 5/5, `sampled: true` | 0.10/0.18 s | **405/468 MiB** |

The measurement earned its keep: **my first 256 MiB default was wrong** — that 249 MB CSV passes it and still OOMs. 128 MiB comes from the measured ~8–9× bytes→RSS expansion and lands on the W3 pass/fail boundary.

## Tests

**4056 passed / 1 skipped, 97.22% coverage.** `sampling.py` 100%, `unity_catalog.py` 99%, `flatfile.py` 98%. Black/Ruff/mypy/Bandit all clean locally before push.

Three real defects found by my own tests/measurements and fixed: `take_head` pulled one batch past its limit (a wasted range request on the path that exists to be cheap); the cap default; and a size probe that fired even when the cap was disabled.

## Deferred

- **Live UC verification pending (orchestrator)** — `TABLESAMPLE`'s behaviour is a Databricks fact; per #953 only a live run is evidence. The SQL DataQ builds is unit-pinned; the flat-file half is measured.
- Iceberg sampling (excluded rather than half-supported), column projection for flat-file monitors, and incremental/delta-only validation (out of scope by design — a design note is in §W6: a watermark belongs beside `sampling` with the same result-record shape).
- UI surfacing is the #318 batch's; the API returns everything a badge needs.

One process note worth carrying: an unstubbed UC count probe doesn't *fail* a test — it opens a real Databricks session to the fake host and retries for 15 minutes, so the suite reports a timeout instead of a defect. That cost me one 921 s test run before I found it; both affected tests now stub it with a comment saying why.</result>

test: migration-parity literal-set check can't distinguish IS NULL from IS NOT NULL
---
Filed per the working agreement: review findings deferred from a PR are tracked, never silently dropped. Surfaced by \`/code-review\` on #1322 (the #323 retention-sweep index/batch PR).

## The gap

\`backend/tests/db/test_migration_parity.py::test_vocabularies_in_predicates_match_between_model_and_database\` compares partial-index and CHECK-constraint predicates between the SQLAlchemy model and a migration-built database by extracting the set of **quoted string literals** (\`_literals()\`, a regex over \`'...'\`) from each side and diffing the sets.

This misses drift where the predicate's *logic* changes but no literal moves. Concretely: if a future edit inverted \`sample_failures_purged_at IS NULL\` to \`sample_failures_purged_at IS NOT NULL\` on either the model's \`postgresql_where=text(...)\` or the migration's raw SQL — but not both — the literal-set comparison would still pass, because neither clause contains a quoted string literal at all. The same blind spot applies to any predicate built entirely from IS [NOT] NULL / comparison operators with no string literal operand.

## Why it matters here

\`ix_results_unpurged_created\` (added in #1322) has exactly this shape — \`sample_failures_purged_at IS NULL AND sample_failures IS NOT NULL AND jsonb_typeof(sample_failures) <> 'null'\`. The \`'null'\` literal is covered, but the two \`IS [NOT] NULL\` clauses are not: an inversion on one side only would silently pass this test while the index diverges from what the sweep's query actually needs (or from what the model claims), reintroducing the F1/F2-shaped class of bug #1322 exists to close — the sweep quietly stops benefiting from the index it doesn't do a full-scan seq-scan check on.

## Suggested fix

Extend \`test_vocabularies_in_predicates_match_between_model_and_database\` (or add a sibling check) to also normalize and compare the full predicate expression tree — or at minimum extract \`IS [NOT] NULL\` clauses (and other literal-free comparison shapes) the same way \`_literals()\` extracts quoted strings, so a bare polarity flip is caught. The module's own docstring already frames this as "the drift \`compare_metadata\` cannot see" — this is the same category of gap the module exists to close, just not yet covered for this specific predicate shape.

## Not blocking
